Toxicology Chapter 200

Caustic Ingestions

Caustic ingestion is an airway-first problem with delayed structural consequences. The board hinge is not oral pain alone; it is drooling, stridor, vomiting, food refusal, intentional ingestion, shock, chest pain, peritonitis, and whether the patient needs early endoscopy, CT, ICU, nutrition, or surgery.

Board lens: do not give charcoal, ipecac, blind NG tubes, dilution, or neutralization. Protect the airway, protect staff, define injury depth, and admit symptomatic or high-grade injuries.

Common Compounds

AlkalisDrain openers, oven cleaners, cement, batteries, bleach. Mechanism: liquefaction necrosis.
AcidsBatteries, drain openers, toilet cleaners, hydrofluoric acid. Mechanism: coagulation necrosis.
Bleach nuanceHousehold 3-6% sodium hypochlorite is often low risk; industrial bleach is not.
PodsLaundry pods can cause vomiting, respiratory distress, neurologic depression, and aspiration.
Tintinalli Table 200-1
Rosen source check

Rosen Ch.55 Key Concepts: Acid/Alkali Chemical Injury

Rosen Ch.55 is not a GI caustic-ingestion chapter, but its acid/alkali chemical-injury principles are directly relevant to exposure control and ED safety.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Tintinalli Ch.200 is focused on ingested caustics, endoscopy, CT, perforation, and stricture risk. Rosen emphasizes route-agnostic chemical injury: concentration, contact time, acid vs alkali properties, HazMat control, and decontamination before definitive ED evaluation.

Pathophysiology and Clinical Features

Alkali injuryProtein denaturation, lipid saponification, thrombosis, deeper penetration, esophageal injury.
Acid injuryCoagulation necrosis; gastric necrosis/perforation/hemorrhage can occur; systemic acidosis, hemolysis, renal failure possible.
Airway signsHoarseness, stridor, dyspnea, drooling, pharyngeal burns, coughing, wheeze.
GI dangerDysphagia, odynophagia, chest pain, epigastric tenderness, vomiting, peritoneal signs.
Tintinalli Figures 200-1 and 200-2

Diagnosis

Intentional ingestions are high risk with or without obvious oral injury. In children with unintentional exposure, serious injuries are usually symptomatic; concerning signs include stridor, drooling, vomiting, food refusal, significant oropharyngeal burns, or respiratory distress.

Endoscopy: traditional gold standard for esophagus, stomach, and duodenum; perform early when indicated, ideally within 12 to 24 hours. Tissue friability rises after 24-48 hours and is maximal days 5-14.
Tintinalli Table 200-2

For intentional or strong acid/alkali exposures, evaluate for acidosis, bleeding, organ injury, and co-ingestants: blood gas, electrolytes, CBC, lactate, hepatic profile, type and screen, and acetaminophen/salicylate levels in suicidal patients. Chest radiograph is useful for chest pain, dyspnea, or vomiting; IV contrasted thoracoabdominal CT can help evaluate injury depth and surgical risk.

Treatment

ED treatment starts with airway assessment, exposure control, and early risk stratification for endoscopy. Do not be reassured by a quiet mouth: absence of oral burns does not exclude esophageal injury, and intentional ingestions or symptoms such as drooling, dysphagia, vomiting, chest/abdominal pain, stridor, or hematemesis need urgent GI/toxicology coordination.

Immediate care is dilution of the system, not neutralization of the chemical. Remove contaminated clothing, irrigate skin and eyes, control pain and nausea, keep the patient NPO when significant injury is possible, and evaluate for airway edema or perforation. Do not induce emesis, do not give activated charcoal routinely, and do not attempt acid-base neutralization because heat generation and vomiting can worsen injury.

AirwayEarly secure airway for respiratory distress. Prefer oral intubation with direct visualization; prepare for difficult airway/cricothyrotomy.
Staff safetyGowns, gloves, masks/face shields; remove contaminated clothing; copious irrigation for skin/eyes.
AvoidActivated charcoal, ipecac, blind NG tube, dilution, neutralization.
ShockLarge-bore IV access, crystalloid resuscitation, treat bleeding/co-ingestants/metabolic disarray.
Steroids and antibiotics: evidence is controversial. No clear routine role; consider only with specialist guidance, specific grade/institutional protocols, or infection/perforation concerns.
Rosen source check

Rosen Ch.55. Decontamination and Neutralization Trap

Rosen's management section explains why caustic care begins with controlled decontamination rather than chemical counter-reactions.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Tintinalli says avoid dilution/neutralization in GI caustic ingestion and prioritize airway plus early GI/surgery planning. Rosen adds the external-exposure mechanics: remove clothing, brush dry chemicals before water, irrigate with large-volume low-pressure water, and avoid neutralization because heat/tissue injury can worsen.
Rosen figure/table audit

GI Caustic Ingestion-Specific Rosen Figure/Table

Within Rosen Ch.55 Chemical Injuries, I found no figure/table dedicated specifically to swallowed caustic ingestion equivalent to Tintinalli Ch.200 endoscopic grading or CT/management tables.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: For actual GI caustic ingestion, Tintinalli remains the chapter spine. Rosen is kept only where it changes ED handling: acid/alkali injury mechanics, staff safety, external decontamination, and the neutralization trap. I removed Rosen Table 55.1 because it is an ocular-burn grading table, and removed Rosen Box 55.1 because phone-number boxes do not add learning value here.

Drug Dose Reference

This section is only a recap after the clinical treatment pathway above. Caustic ingestion has no reversal antidote; medications are supportive, procedural, or complication-directed. Endoscopy timing and airway control matter more than any drug dose.

InterventionUseBoard Notes
Oxygen / early definitive airwayRespiratory distress, stridor, progressive edema, aspirationAirway is first priority; direct visualization preferred.
Isotonic crystalloid bolusesShock from bleeding, third spacing, perforation, co-ingestants, acidosisEscalate monitoring/central access as needed.
Analgesia and antiemeticsPain control; reduce vomiting/re-exposureAvoid inducing emesis.
AntibioticsNot prophylactic routinelyUse for infection, perforation, surgical indications, or specialist protocol.
CorticosteroidsControversial for stricture preventionNot routine; discuss with GI/surgery/toxicology.

Disposition and Follow-Up

DischargeLow-risk, asymptomatic, no drooling/stridor/vomiting, tolerates PO after observation.
AdmitAll symptomatic caustic ingestions.
Grade 1May discharge after endoscopy if tolerating food/fluids.
Grade 2AHospitalize to ensure no progression.
Grade 2B / 3ICU; nutrition support; monitor for bleeding/perforation.
Long-termStricture, gastric outlet obstruction, and very high esophageal squamous cancer risk after grade 3 injury.

Inline MCQs

After caustic ingestion with drooling and hoarseness, what is the first priority?

A. Neutralization is not recommended.

B. Airway comes first because edema and laryngotracheal burns can progress.

C. Charcoal is contraindicated for isolated caustics.

D. Blind nasotracheal intubation may worsen injury.

Tintinalli Ch.200: history and treatment-airway.

Which caustic mechanism is typical of alkali ingestion?

A. This better describes strong acids.

B. Alkalis saponify lipids/proteins and can penetrate deeply.

C. Hydrofluoric acid has calcium effects, but that is not the broad alkali mechanism.

D. That is hydrocarbon aspiration.

Tintinalli Ch.200: pathophysiology.

A toddler takes household bleach, has no drooling, stridor, vomiting, or pain, and tolerates oral intake after observation. Best disposition?

A. Low-risk asymptomatic patients who tolerate PO can be discharged after observation.

B. ICU is for high-grade/symptomatic injury.

C. Common household bleach is usually low risk unless symptoms/significant exposure.

D. Ipecac/vomiting is contraindicated.

Tintinalli Ch.200: disposition.

Who should undergo early endoscopy regardless of symptoms?

A. Suicidal/intentional ingestion carries high risk of important injury.

B. Unintentional low-risk asymptomatic ingestions are more selective.

C. CT can be adjunctive but not this rule.

D. Neutralization is not recommended.

Tintinalli Ch.200: endoscopy indications.

Best timing for endoscopy when indicated after caustic ingestion?

A. Experts recommend early endoscopy within 12 to 24 hours.

B. Friability rises after 24-48 hours and is maximal days 5-14.

C. Too late for acute grading.

D. Endoscopy can guide feeding tube placement.

Tintinalli Ch.200: endoscopy timing.

Which is contraindicated when caustic is the only ingestion?

A. Staff protection is appropriate.
